# Paper Framing — gen-depth-fingerprint

## Target Venue
- Primary: AAAI 2027 (deadline: August 2, 2026)
- **Primary: EMNLP 2026 ARR (deadline: May 25, 2026)** — D012: 恢复为主投稿目标
- Fallback venues: ICLR 2027 (Sep 24), NAACL 2027 ARR (Oct 16)

## Core Insight
Non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains exhibit **differential depth response**: **central-tendency/diversity features** (entropy_mean, TTR, hapax ratio) drift monotonically with depth, while **distributional shape features** (entropy_std, tail_decay) remain near-stationary. This differential response is consistent with recursive generation inducing a **location shift** in the NLL distribution — the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts) while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant). The genuine novelty is not the drift/stationarity split per se (which follows from location-shift properties), but: (a) the **task formulation** (ordinal depth estimation beyond binary detection), (b) **empirical validation** across 6 generators / 3 model families (including 7B+ scale) showing this pattern is robust, (c) the practical consequence that combining both feature types yields **complementary signal** for depth classification (macro-F1 0.79 cross-generator with 6 generators, 0.77 cross-family). Depth signal is scale-invariant as a phenomenon, though cross-scale classifier transfer shows a moderate gap (8B held-out F1=0.69 vs ≤2.8B 0.76-0.85).

## Core Claims (3 条，均可证伪)

**Claim 1 — Depth Discriminability**: Distributional features computed under a held-out reference model can classify text generation depth (gen-0 / gen-1 / gen-2+) with macro-F1 significantly above chance, generalizing across unseen generators (leave-one-generator-out evaluation).

**Claim 2 — Differential Depth Response & Feature Complementarity**: Depth-dependent features exhibit differential response: central-tendency/diversity features (entropy_mean, TTR, hapax_ratio) drift monotonically with depth (consistent with location shift in NLL distribution), while shape features (entropy_std, tail_decay) remain near-stationary. Full feature set (cross-gen 0.80) significantly outperforms surface-only (0.75) and reference-only (0.75) — the two feature groups are complementary. Notably, reference features generalize better across generators while surface features are stronger in-distribution — demonstrating complementarity across different evaluation axes.

**Claim 3 — Downstream Utility (Negative Finding)**: Depth-aware data curation does NOT improve downstream CLM quality compared to random subsampling. At equal data count, size_matched (random control, ppl=2.367) outperforms depth01 (depth-stratified, 2.387) and binary_filtered (2.389). The primary determinant is data quantity, not depth composition (all 12K samples → ppl=2.335). Depth fingerprinting is an effective **diagnostic** tool for characterizing provenance, but not a **curative** tool for data curation. This honest negative finding is reported transparently.

## Story Spine

**Problem**: Web-scraped training data increasingly contains LLM-generated text of unknown provenance depth. Current detection methods offer only binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing all-or-nothing filtering: discard everything flagged as synthetic (losing useful gen-1 content) or keep everything (admitting high-risk deep-generation text with compounding distributional drift).

**Existing approaches & gaps**: Binary detectors (FastDetectGPT, SynthID-Text, LD-Score) cannot distinguish gen-1 from gen-2+. Attractor cycle theory (ACL 2025) proves paraphrasing chains converge to 2-period cycles, bounding depth signal to ~3 classes — but this result depends on the semantic-preservation constraint of paraphrasing. No existing work attempts generation depth estimation. When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, single detector scores (Avg-LogProb 0.77, LD-Score 0.72) show moderate signal but **high cross-generator variance** (CIs spanning 0.41–0.82), making them unreliable as standalone depth estimators.

**Our framing**: We characterize distributional drift in recursive non-paraphrastic LLM generation, revealing **differential depth response**: level/diversity features (including reference-model entropy_mean) drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape features (entropy variance, tail decay) remain near-stationary. This split is about **what the feature measures** (central tendency vs shape), not where it comes from. The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble (LOGO F1=0.80 [0.786, 0.799]) that **significantly and consistently** outperforms all single-detector baselines (p<0.001 vs Avg-LogProb 0.77, LD-Score 0.72, FastDetectGPT 0.63, Binoculars 0.58). Crucially, single detectors exhibit high cross-generator variance (CIs spanning 0.41–0.82), while our ensemble maintains tight consistency — the practical advantage is **reliability across unknown generators**, not just average performance.

**Headline result template**: "On multi-generator continuation chains across 6 generators from 3 model families (0.6B–8.2B), our 7-feature distributional ensemble achieves 6-gen LOGO macro-F1 of 0.79 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86. Depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling for downstream CLM quality, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization, not a curative tool for data selection."

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns

**RC1 — "Is this just vocabulary impoverishment?"**: Surface features alone achieve 0.73 macro-F1, but full features achieve 0.79 (p<0.001). We don't claim reference features are "better" — we show they capture a **different, complementary** signal (stationary distributional shape vs drifting level/diversity). The dual dynamics finding is itself a scientific contribution. Note: "fingerprint" in the paper refers to the full feature vector's combination, not just reference-model features.

**RC7 — Pre-registered prediction (LD-Score)**: LD-Score (character-distribution signature) measures character-level distributional properties. We predict it is a **level feature** (sensitive to vocabulary/character frequency shifts) and should exhibit **H₂ drift** with depth. This prediction is registered before plan_011 execution as an out-of-sample test of the level/shape framework.

**RC2 — "Does this generalize beyond Pythia?"**: MVP used same-family models (Pythia-2.8B generator + Pythia-410M reference). → Cross-family experiments: Qwen/OLMo generators + non-Pythia reference models (RQ1 cross-generator evaluation).

**RC3 — "Is 3-class sufficient? Why not finer-grained?"**: Attractor theory bounds paraphrasing to ~3 classes. → Secondary analysis: finer-grained ordinal classification (gen-0 through gen-4) on non-paraphrastic chains to test if more depth signal exists.

**RC4 — "How realistic are single-model chains?"**: Real web contamination involves diverse generators. → Cross-model chains (different generator per depth step) as primary evaluation setting (RQ3).

**RC5 — "What about human editing / post-processing?"**: Real-world synthetic text is often edited. → Robustness test with simulated human edits (random word replacement as lower-bound + LLM-simulated editing).

**RC6 — "Ecological validity — continuation vs real web content"**: Lab-constructed chains may not match wild distribution. → Multi-domain seeds (news, Wikipedia, scientific, creative) + multiple prompt types (continuation, elaboration, inspired rewriting).

**RC8 — "Aren't these just OOD detection features?"**: Reference-model entropy statistics are functionally NLL-based OOD scores (same signal backbone as DetectGPT/GLTR/Binoculars). Our contribution is NOT the features themselves but: (a) the problem formulation (ordinal depth estimation, not binary detection), (b) the empirical discovery that these features exhibit dual dynamics (level drift vs shape stationarity) under recursive generation, and (c) the practical application to risk-stratified data curation. Paper must explicitly connect to OOD detection + perplexity-based detection literature and position the contribution as primarily empirical/conceptual rather than methodological.

**RC9 — "Only ≤2.8B generators — does this transfer to frontier scale?"**: **Answered (plan-014, D011).** Qwen3-8B (7.6B params) added as 6th generator. Depth signal IS present at 8B scale — all feature-depth Spearman correlations significant (hapax ρ=-0.568, ttr ρ=-0.553, entropy_mean ρ=-0.475, all p<1e-6), confirming depth fingerprinting is a scale-invariant phenomenon. However, cross-scale transfer shows a gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1=0.69 vs ≤2.8B generators 0.76-0.85 (6-gen LOGO average 0.7886, -1.1pp from 5-gen 0.80). Notably, adding 8B data improves original 5-gen classification (+0.9pp to 0.8086). **Paper framing**: depth signal universality is supported (Claim 1 holds); cross-scale classifier transfer gap reported as honest limitation with analysis (8B text is more fluent → smaller feature margins → harder to distinguish from human text). The 6-gen LOGO 0.79 still significantly outperforms all single-detector baselines.

**RC10 — "Text length confound"**: Hapax ratio and TTR are mechanically length-dependent. If generation chains produce texts of systematically different lengths, surface features may track length artifacts rather than distributional drift. → Length distribution analysis + length-normalized features + length-matched comparison (plan_013). Critical confound control.

**RC11 — "Downstream utility — single run, no CIs"**: Depth-aware filtering advantage must be validated with multiple seeds + bootstrap CIs + sample-count-matched comparison (to control for data size confound). Must use non-Pythia model for downstream fine-tuning (OLMo-1B) to avoid reference model circularity (Pythia-410M as both feature extractor and eval model).

## Contribution Positioning (D006+D007)
The contribution is **primarily empirical and conceptual**, not methodological:
1. **Problem formulation**: Ordinal depth estimation as a new task beyond binary detection (genuinely novel — no prior work)
2. **Empirical characterization**: Differential depth response across 6 generators / 3 families (including 7B+ scale), with robust cross-generator generalization (6-gen LOGO 0.79, family-out 0.77). Scale-invariant phenomenon with honest cross-scale transfer gap.
3. **Negative finding**: Depth-aware data curation does NOT improve downstream CLM quality — depth fingerprinting is diagnostic, not curative (D009).

**Framing discipline (D007 — re-dream consensus):**
- Do NOT call the drift/stationarity split a "discovery" — it follows from location-shift properties of the NLL distribution (means shift under distributional drift, shapes don't). Acknowledge this explicitly.
- Do NOT use H1/H2 terminology (overloads time-series unit-root convention). Use "drifting" vs "stationary" or "differential response."
- Do NOT overclaim "dual dynamics" as a novel theoretical framework. Use "differential depth response" — more calibrated.
- Consider renaming "distributional fingerprinting" → "distributional depth profiling" (fingerprinting implies source identification, creates confusion with LLM attribution literature).
- Provide at least a speculative theoretical motivation for WHY shape features remain stationary (e.g., "shape is determined by sampling mechanism and architecture, invariant to input content drift").
- Report **realistic performance range** (0.69–0.85 per-generator held-out F1, 0.79 LOGO average across 6 generators) in abstract/conclusion, not just best-case.
- R² on 5 aggregated depth means is statistically meaningless (3 df). Use individual-level Spearman ρ with bootstrap CIs throughout.

Related work must expand to 30+ references covering: perplexity-based detection (DetectGPT, GLTR, DNA-GPT, Binoculars), model collapse theory (Alemohammad et al., Dohmatob et al., Gerstgrasser et al., Guo et al.), OOD detection (Hendrycks & Gimpel), data quality scoring (DSIR, QuRating, CCNet), watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al.), vocabulary diversity (Guo et al. 2024, Padmakumar & He 2024, Holtzman et al. 2020), **stylometry/authorship attribution** (Stamatatos 2009, Koppel et al. 2009 — feature set is essentially stylometric), **iterative generation** (LLM as Broken Telephone ACL 2025, Markovian Generation Chains), **membership inference** (Shi et al. 2024).

## Venue Fit
- AAAI 2027: Fit as empirical + conceptual contribution — novel task formulation (depth estimation) + surprising empirical finding (dual dynamics) + practical application (data curation). Must position as empirical science, not methodology paper.
- EMNLP 2026: Excellent fit — directly addresses special theme "New Missions for NLP Research" (data contamination, synthetic data feedback loops, data governance). NLP-native venue for text-focused work. Empirical/conceptual contributions better received here than AAAI.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary synthetic text detection, providing a framework for characterizing the provenance of web-crawled text at finer granularity.
Across six generators from three model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), we documented differential depth response: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble combining both feature types achieves leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 of 0.79, with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
We also reported that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic rather than curative tool.

Future work should extend evaluation to frontier-scale generators (70B+), mixed-generator chains that better approximate real-world contamination, and multilingual settings.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables risk-stratified data curation.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can flag gen-2+ text for manual review while retaining gen-1 content that preserves much of the source distribution's properties.
Three-class granularity is well-suited to this use case: it separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to curation decisions.
Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.
The tight cross-generator consistency of the ensemble (CI width 1.4\,pp) makes deployment feasible even when the generating model is unknown.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
As large language model (LLM) outputs accumulate on the web, training corpora increasingly contain recursively generated text of unknown provenance depth.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying whether text is human-written (gen-0), first-generation synthetic (gen-1), or deeper (gen-2+)---a task that moves beyond binary real-versus-synthetic detection.
Existing detectors provide only binary scores and, when repurposed for ordinal prediction, exhibit high cross-generator variance (confidence intervals spanning 0.41--0.82), making them unreliable depth estimators.
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response} in distributional features computed under a held-out reference model: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy mean, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay rate) remain near-stationary.
Combining both feature types into a 7-feature ensemble exploits this complementarity: the full set (macro-F1\,=\,0.79) outperforms surface-only (0.73) and reference-only (0.75) subsets.
In leave-one-generator-out evaluation across 6 generators from 3 model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), the ensemble achieves macro-F1 of 0.79 ($p < 0.001$ vs.\ all single-detector baselines), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
However, depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language modeling quality compared to random subsampling---data quantity, not depth composition, is the primary determinant---positioning depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization, not a curative tool for data selection.
\end{abstract}

1	% Appendix A — Length Confound Analysis
2	% Data source: plan-013 (23,032 samples, 5 generators)
3	
4	Surface diversity features (TTR, hapax ratio) mechanically depend on text length:
5	shorter texts yield higher type-token ratios by construction.
6	If generation depth systematically shortens text, observed depth trends could be length artifacts rather than genuine distributional shifts.
7	We rule this out with three complementary analyses.
8	
9	\paragraph{(a) Length--depth correlation.}
10	We compute Spearman rank correlation between word count and depth across all five generators.
11	Correlations are weak and inconsistent in sign:
12	$\rho$ ranges from $-0.066$ (Pythia-1B) to $+0.134$ (OLMo-2-1B), with $|\rho| < 0.14$ in every case.
13	One generator (Qwen3-0.6B) shows no significant correlation ($\rho = 0.012$, $p = 0.43$).
14	Length and depth are thus near-independent in our corpus.
15	
16	\paragraph{(b) Length-normalized feature trends.}
17	To eliminate residual length effects, we recompute TTR and hapax ratio on fixed 200-word windows.
18	After normalization, monotonic depth trends are fully preserved for all generators; moreover, Spearman correlations between normalized features and depth \emph{increase} in absolute value (e.g., Pythia-2.8B TTR: $\rho = -0.633 \to -0.715$).
19	Length removal sharpens the depth signal rather than diminishing it, confirming that the signal is not a length artifact.
20	
21	\paragraph{(c) Length-matched classification.}
22	We subsample the dataset so that word-count distributions are equalized across depth classes, then retrain the 3-class XGBoost classifier (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}).
23	Macro-F1 changes by $\Delta = +0.041$ relative to the unmatched baseline---performance \emph{improves} when length variance is removed.
24	This is consistent with length acting as noise rather than signal.
25	
26	\paragraph{Conclusion.}
27	We observe a dropout bias: shorter texts are more likely to fall below the minimum-length threshold at deeper generation stages.
28	However, this bias does not drive the depth fingerprint.
29	All three analyses converge on the same conclusion: the depth signal captured by our feature ensemble is independent of text-length variation.

To eliminate residual length effects, we recompute TTR and hapax ratio on fixed 200-word windows.

Length removal sharpens the depth signal rather than diminishing it, confirming that the signal is not a length artifact.

\paragraph{(c) Length-matched classification.}
We subsample the dataset so that word-count distributions are equalized across depth classes, then retrain the 3-class XGBoost classifier (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}).
Macro-F1 changes by $\Delta = +0.041$ relative to the unmatched baseline---performance \emph{improves} when length variance is removed.
This is consistent with length acting as noise rather than signal.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
We observe a dropout bias: shorter texts are more likely to fall below the minimum-length threshold at deeper generation stages.
However, this bias does not drive the depth fingerprint.
All three analyses converge on the same conclusion: the depth signal captured by our feature ensemble is independent of text-length variation.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
\label{sec:related-detection}

Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests on token-level distributions \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot approaches exploiting reference-model likelihoods \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers over linguistic features \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
Recent work has pursued diverse detection signals: \citet{intrinsic_dimension} use intrinsic dimensionality estimates, \citet{diveye} propose surprisal diversity features directly comparable to our shape-based measures, and \citet{generator_barrier} characterize the distributional gap between human and model outputs.
\citet{jawahar_survey} provide a comprehensive survey.
A persistent limitation is that all these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
Even when detection scores correlate with generation depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance when repurposed as ordinal predictors (CI spanning 0.41--0.82 in macro-F1; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), because each score captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently.
\citet{paraphrase_evades} and \citet{detection_possibilities} further demonstrate that detection robustness degrades under distributional shift.
Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}; the contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the empirical finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
\label{sec:related-collapse}

A growing body of work studies quality degradation when models are trained on their own outputs.
\citet{self_consuming_mad} demonstrate that self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage, and \citet{curse_of_recursion} show that model collapse is inevitable in successive fine-tuning rounds without fresh human data, though \citet{model_collapse_avoidable} identify conditions under which careful data mixing can mitigate this effect.
\citet{strong_model_collapse} extend these results to larger-scale settings.
These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation, where model weights are updated on recursive data.
Our setting is different: we study \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.

Two concurrent lines of work are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss analogous to the telephone game.
\citet{markovian_chains} provide a theoretical framework for convergence in iterative text transformations, demonstrating that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics that bound distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
Our work differs in two respects: we study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal beyond the attractor bound; and we focus on \emph{estimating} depth from text features rather than characterizing convergence behavior.

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
Our surface features---type-token ratio and hapax ratio---instantiate this observation for inference chains, where we show monotonic diversity decline across generation depths without any model retraining.

These features are classical stylometric measures with a long history in authorship attribution \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}.
\citet{uchendu_attribution} extend stylometric and neural methods to multi-class attribution of text to specific generators.
We push beyond generator identity to the \emph{depth} dimension: text from the same generator at different depths exhibits systematically different feature profiles, and these profiles generalize across generators.
